I'm sure you can figure out how to run NetBSD as a guest OS on an LPAR (what IBM calls a virtual machine), but to my knowledge it hasn't been compiled as a host OS. In this case, it's not a trivial task, to just download and build a kernel. The kernel itself has to be altered to support a different type of processor. For instance, Linux will run on Sparc, x86_64, i686, IA64 and now Z. Each type of processor is a different instruction set.

What makes this interesting is that in the past, IBM forced you to use z/OS for the base operating system which itself is a UNIX in the broad sense of the word. Now Linux is certified to run as the native OS.

The reason you will never see OpenBSD or NetBSD running as the native OS on an IBM mainframe is simply because it isn't certified or supported. It's not to say that they couldn't port the OS to the processor, but at a few million bucks each, the businesses that buy them aren't going to run an unsupported OS on it.
